full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN. The flipping is mostly a known side effect of updating every cell at once, not a new emergent pattern.**

I agree with the first pass's KNOWN label, but not with its reasoning. The only feature that passed the checks is g_reversals (cells flipping back and forth). The first pass explained the domain structure using frozen three-way junctions (T-junctions) in 3-state Potts dynamics. Frozen junctions are the opposite of flipping, so that explanation doesn't cover the feature actually under test.

**Where the reversals come from.** Your own sub-program table settles this:
- Rule 2 alone (majority vote, all cells updated at once) gives 0.85.
- The full program gives 0.58.
- Rule 3 alone (agents advancing the cell under them) gives 0.36.
- Rule 1 alone gives 0.

So majority voting on its own produces *more* flipping than the full system. Adding the agents reduces it. Nothing new appears when the rules are combined. The knock-out comparison (0.58 vs 0) looks impressive only because removing interactions also removes rule 2, since rule 2 reads neighbouring cells.

**Why majority voting flips.** This is a classic result. For finite symmetric threshold networks, Goles and Olivos established the classical period-two property: every trajectory eventually reaches a fixed point or a cycle of period two. On a lattice, every trajectory on a finite torus eventually reaches a fixed point or a cycle of length two. In plain terms, cells either settle or end up changing in every round. The result also holds with more than two types: Goles and Olivos and independently Poljak and Sura proved that a large class of majority-based models, including (biased) majority model, always reach a cycle of period one or two. It is a product of updating every cell at the same time. Whereas 2-cycles cannot emerge under the sequential model, in the synchronous model… 2-cycles exist even for r=1.

**What rule 3 adds.** Agents advance the type of a cell, and majority voting then pushes it back. That produces back-and-forth flips along the agents' paths, which is just a disturbance being repaired, not a pattern.

**Genuine or artifact?** Artifact. The feature combines period-2 blinking caused by simultaneous updating with agents disturbing cells that the majority rule then restores. Rule 1 (flocking) has no measurable effect on this feature: rules 1+3 give 0.33 vs 0.36 for rule 3 alone, and rules 1+2 match rule 2 alone at 0.85. A simple test would be to rerun with cells updated one at a time. If the reversals mostly disappear, the artifact explanation is confirmed.

I ran one search, for the Goles–Olivos period-two theorem on synchronous majority automata. It returned several independent sources confirming it.
